title: The UAE embraces AI for kindergartners
source_used: Rest of World (own reporting, full text read)
key_facts: The United Arab Emirates recently became the first country to make AI a required K-12 subject (Rest of World).

UAE schools mostly treat AI as literacy, not technical training: at Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, students in grades one to three do not use generative AI independently; teachers use discussions, stories and role-play, for example showing something an AI got wrong or acting as a robot taking instructions.
Older students have restricted access to school-approved apps; schools monitor apps and use firewalls, and do not currently allow public ChatGPT accounts in school (principal James Efford).
The government plans to train 22,000 teachers to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis and lesson planning.

Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is developing a broader policy framework and a 10-year roadmap; Abu Dhabi's education department, writing the framework for more than 170 private schools, did not respond.

By contrast, New York City introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from preschool to grade eight, citing mental health concerns, and Norway enacted a similar near-ban for primary school; China has trained 2.97 million teachers in AI over eight years, per its education ministry.
Some parents said they were not consulted but supported it; one asked for details on tools used and data privacy.

Edward Tsoi, CEO and co-founder of AI Safety Asia, a nonprofit, says children need to struggle with hard tasks first and urged a 'hard line between teaching AI and handing children an AI tool'; he says the UAE's small, well-funded, centralised system is hard for others to copy.
quote_evidence: The United Arab Emirates recently became the first country to make AI a required K-12 subject.
The UAE's approach is not to give young children unrestricted access to AI. Instead, schools teach them how the technology works, where it fails, and when humans should use it.
The government plans to train 22,000 teachers to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning.
why_it_matters_hint: A whole national school system now teaches AI from the earliest years, while other countries restrict it for young children.
event_date: Feature published 13 Oct 2026; the national mandate is described as 'recent' with no date
notes: The date of the UAE mandate is not given in the article, so freshness is treated as new. Single outlet; Abu Dhabi's education department did not respond; no evidence on learning outcomes is reported.
